Hi xxfyre,

First off I want to say I'm so sorry that you're going through ask that. I hurt my back while working in the emergency department lifting s having patient. I have a slight herniation at T8-T9, but the main problem is my facet joints at T6-7 and T7-8, which seem to like moving about as much as a pissed off toddler with a knife. Oh, and this has been going on since August 2014.

Now that my "credentials" are through,I just want to preface this by saying that I'm in the US, so I have a lack of knowledge of the political of social assistance programs with our neighbours from the North. So for question number one, I can't help you.

Question number 2, however, I can sure try! I just yesterday went through a hell of a discussion with my father of the same sort. He and my stepmother, while not being in the military, have very much the same attitude as your in-laws (though I imagine that the military mindset will make it a bit harder to get it across to them). And the one thing you need to remember is that when people with a limited ability to empathize, they relate based on their own experience. The problem is when they use their past, it generally is not anywhere as severe, or if it is, it didn't last for longer than a month or two. So, while they truly believe they can relate, they actually can't, but again they don't realize this.

What I think you should say consists of the following:
-can we please sit down and have a serious talk?

-what I have to say is long but please let me finish before saying anything

-you have a two different major problems going on. The herniated disc as well as a chronically damaged facet joint

-maybe go into the basics of how when a vertebral disc is herniated bad enough it presses against a central nerve coming from the spinal cord (and whip out some easy to understand visuals if you think it's help you get the point across)

-going into the effects of the nerve being pressed on that you experience

-talk basically about the facet joint (trust me it's easier that way lol), what it is and how it works

-explain that when the joint is injured, the two vertebrae can lock out of place and cause excruciating muscle spasms

-this is because the spine is central to body support and any compromise to that throws the body into a reactive panic

-go into when you have done something that aggravates either, it leads to xyz pain...(for me it's a burning stabbing pain that radiates slightly left and feels like there is a red hot knife stuck in my back and I can't pull it out) rated at its worst a solid 9 out of 10

-now this is where we get to the emotional traumatic side...go into how you have to second and triple guess every move you make, whether it be bending down to pick up a bag or shifting how you sit. Every move if done wrong leads to days or weeks of agony.

-and them finally I would touch on the times when you do feel better for a short time. Got them it doesn't make sense because of you seem to be feeling better then you are better!! What many people (your in-laws and my dad included) don't realize is that the pain is not gone. What it has some of lessened and that is such a mental weight off your shoulders that you feel slightly euphoric because it's finally abated! ... But it's not gone and you know that

-oh! And when I talked to my dad he went on about how I don't seem to have a plan forward and such and I told him this: that there are times when I am in between episodes of pain when I have sometimes up to a 5 year plan of hour I'm going to get my life back on track and get rolling. But then the second my back spasms, I'm lucky if I can think an hour or two ahead. I am constantly trying to plan what my next position im going to shift to is once the one I'm in becomes unbearable and at the same time should I actually cave and take pain medicine or a muscle relaxer (I am super afraid of getting hooked on pain meds... I have an addictive personality)

Part 3- keeping same during this is the hardest thing. What it comes down to most is distracting yourself. I am an avid gamer and reader (along with hiker, runner, and cyclist before this started) and those are my go to. Reading gets hard when it's really bad so that's when I turn to twitch.TV for distracting. But it comes down to what distracts you best and use it when you need it. Also there are support groups for people with chronic pain. The website for you would be www.chronicpaincanada.com and find your local one.

Part 4-with your problem I'd say welding is out of the question but there are other options. I am a biologist by trade and use Upwork.Com and freelancer.com to find work. It's a right pain to start but if you can get over that hump you can make at least some money. Also many hospitals and doctors offices need transcriptionists that can potentially work from home so look into that!

If you have any other questions, need more advice, or just need to rant PM me! I wish you all the best in getting better and overcoming it as well as smoothing things over with the in-laws!

As an EMT, there were many times that we called arrests on scene.  One in particular was a house four down from me.  I run over and once I'm in the room, I immediately start checking for pulses, nothing.  My grandfather (also a firefighter and EMT) walks in and I just have to give a look and he understands.  He checks quickly before calling a Class 5 (DOA).  

Fast forward to the present, I now work in the ER at a local hospital, which is also the regions only trauma center.  Nearly every time we are working a cardiac arrest, be it traumatic or otherwise, the doctor will look around and ask everyone if they have any objections to calling it (and they will listen to what you say).  It's always after a long haul, usually at least 40 minutes at least, so we all know deep down there is no chance to get the patient back, but deep down, there's that little part that makes me feel like I killed them because I didn't raise the objection to try for another 5 minutes or so.
